title: C: Array Functions That Return a Value
description: Writing functions that read an array and hand one number back to main().
congratsText: Well done. You can now write a function that works out a value from an array, reuse what it returns, and pick a return type that fits.
objectives: Write a function that returns one number worked out from an array
Keep a returned value in a variable and reuse it
Choose a return type that fits the answer being sent back
Add an extra parameter so one function answers many questions
recap: A function's return type says what it hands back; return is how the answer leaves.
A returned value can be stored and reused, and the size decides how far the loop goes.
int divided by int drops the decimals before any float return type sees it.
Start a counter at zero above the loop, build it up, then return it.

sections.title: A Function That Gives a Number Back

chunks.text: The first word of the function is its return type. int total(...) means it hands a whole number back to whoever called it.

check.question: What does the word int at the front of a function tell you?
options: It sends one whole number back
It only takes whole numbers in

chunks.text: The adding happens in a loop, but the answer leaves through return sum;. Without that line, nothing gets back to main().

check.question: You delete return sum; but keep the loop. What does main() get?
options: Some number nobody can rely on
The correct total, from the loop

chunks.text: The call goes where a number would go. printf("%d", total(scores, 5)); runs the function first, then prints what came back.

check.question: In that printf, what does %d actually print?
options: Whatever total sent back
The address that scores holds

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: 433, the five scores added up
5, the size that was passed in
90, the first item of the array
An address, since arr[] holds one

sections.title: Using the Value That Comes Back

chunks.text: You can keep the answer instead of printing it straight away: int classTotal = total(scores, 5);. The loop runs once, and the number is yours to reuse.

check.question: You print classTotal twice. How many times does the loop run?
options: Once, when total was called
Twice, once per printf line

chunks.text: The size you pass decides how far the loop goes. Same array, smaller size, smaller answer.

check.question: The array holds 5 items but you call total(scores, 3). What happens?
options: It adds the first three only
It adds all five items anyway

chunks.text: A function can hand its job to another one. average() has no loop — it just asks total() for the sum.

check.question: average() has no loop of its own. Can it still work?
options: Yes, total does the looping
No, every function needs one

sections.title: Making the Return Type Fit the Answer

chunks.text: total(arr, size) / size divides an int by an int. C throws the decimals away before the float return type ever sees the answer.

check.question: 433 / 5 in C, with both sides int, gives you what?
options: 86, with the rest dropped
86.6, kept as written

chunks.text: Writing (float) total(arr, size) / size makes one side a float first, so the division keeps its decimals.

check.question: What does putting (float) in front change?
options: How the division is worked out
How printf lays the number out

chunks.text: This bug compiles with no warning at all. A quiet Compile Log only means the code is legal, not that it is right.

check.question: Your program builds with no errors. Is the answer correct?
options: Not always, check it yourself
Yes, a clean build proves it

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a function that returns the average as a decimal.

chunks.text: Add a parameter and one function answers many questions: countAbove(arr, size, limit) works for any limit you hand it.

check.question: Why add a limit parameter instead of writing countAbove86()?
options: One function then covers every limit
It makes the loop finish much faster

chunks.text: The shape never changes: start a counter at zero, loop, then return it. Only what you count is different.

check.question: total returns a sum and countAbove returns a count. What is shared?
options: Both build up a value, then return
Both change items inside the array

chunks.text: Setting the counter to zero inside the loop wipes it every pass. This compiles fine and still gives a wrong count.

check.question: count = 0; sits inside the loop. What comes back?
options: A count of the last item only
The right count, just more slowly

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: 3, since 95, 88 and 91 clear the limit
5, since every item is checked by the loop
2, since only 95 and 91 are far enough up
85, since the limit is what comes back here
